experiments.title: Concurrent Withdrawal Race
experiments.subtitle: Database MVCC & SELECT FOR UPDATE
experiments.scenario: Two API requests arrive simultaneously to withdraw funds from the same account. Without a row-level lock, both reads return the same balance snapshot before either write commits, allowing both to proceed even when only one should.
experiments.impact: A customer with $1,000 could successfully withdraw $800 and $700 simultaneously, leaving the account at $300 instead of the expected $200 — a $500 loss to the institution with no audit trail.
incorrectCode: public void withdraw(Long accountId, BigDecimal amount) {
// UNSAFE: plain SELECT — MVCC snapshot, no row lock
// Race window: another transaction can read the same balance
// between this SELECT and the UPDATE below.

incorrectAnnotations.note: UNSAFE: findById() issues a plain SELECT with no FOR UPDATE clause — PostgreSQL returns the last committed snapshot, so two concurrent transactions both see the same balance.
UNSAFE: the gap between line 17 (read) and line 25 (write) is a race window; a second transaction can read the same balance and pass the balance check before either transaction commits.

experiments.failureExplanation: PostgreSQL's MVCC gives each transaction a consistent snapshot of the database at the moment it starts, so two concurrent transactions both read the same committed balance without blocking each other. Because neither transaction sees the other's uncommitted write, both pass the balance check and both updates succeed, with the second write overwriting the first — a classic lost-update anomaly. The final balance reflects only one of the two withdrawals even though both completed without error.

experiments.performanceNotes: SELECT FOR UPDATE holds a row-level lock for the transaction duration, which serialises writers but does not block readers (unless SKIP LOCKED / NOWAIT is used). Under very high contention (thousands of TPS on one account), lock wait queues grow and p99 latency spikes. The atomic UPDATE approach eliminates the lock window entirely and is the fastest option when only the balance field changes.

assessment.text: Why does PostgreSQL MVCC allow two concurrent transactions to both read the same balance without one blocking the other?
options: A) PostgreSQL uses table-level locks by default for all SELECT statements
B) Each transaction sees a consistent snapshot of committed data taken at transaction start, so plain SELECTs do not block
C) The READ COMMITTED isolation level causes each transaction to wait for the other to finish
D) MVCC only applies to INSERT and DELETE, not UPDATE
assessment.explanation: MVCC gives every transaction a consistent snapshot of the database as of its start time (or statement start under READ COMMITTED). Plain SELECTs never block concurrent writers — they simply read the latest committed version visible to their snapshot. This is why two transactions can both read $1,000 and both pass the balance check before either commits.

assessment.text: What is the minimum change needed to prevent the lost-update race in the withdrawal service?
options: A) Switch the isolation level to SERIALIZABLE on the entire database
B) Add @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) to the repository query so the SELECT acquires a row-level lock
C) Wrap the service method in a Java synchronized block
D) Use @Transactional(readOnly = true) for the read phase
assessment.explanation: Adding PESSIMISTIC_WRITE (which generates SELECT … FOR UPDATE) makes the database acquire a row-level lock before returning the row. Any concurrent transaction that attempts to lock the same row will block until the first transaction commits or rolls back, eliminating the race window.

assessment.text: When should you prefer optimistic locking (@Version) over pessimistic locking (SELECT FOR UPDATE) for balance updates?
options: A) When the account is updated by hundreds of concurrent transactions per second
B) When conflicting updates are rare and the cost of an occasional retry is acceptable
C) When the database does not support row-level locking
D) When you want to prevent dirty reads under READ UNCOMMITTED isolation
assessment.explanation: Optimistic locking avoids holding a lock during the transaction, which is beneficial when conflicts are infrequent. Under high contention, the retry storm caused by frequent ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureExceptions can degrade throughput more than the queuing cost of a row-level lock.

experiments.title: Idempotency Key Race Condition
experiments.subtitle: Check-Then-Act & UNIQUE Constraint
experiments.scenario: A payment client retries a failed request and sends the same idempotency key twice within milliseconds. The service checks whether the key already exists before inserting; two concurrent retries both see 'not found' and both proceed to insert a duplicate payment.
experiments.impact: A customer is charged twice for a single purchase. The merchant receives two settlement entries, support costs spike, and the institution faces regulatory exposure for double-billing without a compensating reversal.
incorrectCode: // UNSAFE: check-then-act — two threads can both see false
// Both threads reach here and both insert a row

incorrectAnnotations.note: UNSAFE: existsByIdempotencyKey() is a non-atomic check; between this line and the save() on line 23, another concurrent transaction can pass the same check and insert a duplicate row.
UNSAFE: both concurrent threads reach this save() after both observed false from existsByIdempotencyKey(), resulting in two payment rows with the same idempotency key.

experiments.failureExplanation: The check (existsByIdempotencyKey) and the act (save) are two separate database operations with no lock or atomic guarantee between them. Under READ COMMITTED isolation, both concurrent transactions execute the SELECT before either INSERT commits, so both see zero matching rows and both proceed to insert. This is a textbook check-then-act race that cannot be fixed by adding retries or synchronised blocks at the application layer — the fix must be enforced at the database level with a UNIQUE constraint.

simulation.bugAnnotation: Both threads passed the existence check before either insert committed, allowing two payment rows with the same idempotency key.

safeSteps.note: T1 inserts payment — UNIQUE constraint in effect
T2 insert violates UNIQUE → DataIntegrityViolationException
T2 catches exception, re-fetches existing payment, returns it ✓

simulation.safeAnnotation: The UNIQUE constraint makes the insert itself atomic and exclusive — the database rejects the second insert, and the application returns the already-committed payment.

correctCode: // DDL: ALTER TABLE payments ADD CONSTRAINT uq_idempotency_key
// UNIQUE constraint fired — duplicate key; return existing
experiments.correctExplanation: By removing the existence check and relying on a database UNIQUE constraint, the insert is the single atomic gate. If two transactions race, the database guarantees exactly one succeeds; the loser catches DataIntegrityViolationException and returns the already-persisted payment instead.

alternatives.whenToUse: Use when you control the database vendor (PostgreSQL/MySQL 8+) and want to avoid exception-driven control flow in the service layer.

experiments.performanceNotes: A UNIQUE index on idempotency_key adds ~1–2 ms to every insert (B-tree index update) but eliminates the extra SELECT from the original check-then-act approach — net result is typically faster and correct. For very high insert volumes, consider a partial index or hash-based index on the key column.

Exception path adds ~1 ms; acceptable for retry scenarios

Log a WARN (not ERROR) when a duplicate key is detected — it is an expected, handled event, not a system failure

assessment.text: Why does adding a Java synchronized block around the existsByIdempotencyKey() + save() calls NOT fix this race condition in a multi-instance deployment?
options: A) synchronized only works for primitive types in Java
B) synchronized serialises threads within one JVM but does nothing to coordinate between multiple application instances sharing the same database
C) Spring @Transactional strips synchronized semantics from the method
D) synchronized blocks prevent the transaction from committing
assessment.explanation: synchronized operates at the JVM level and coordinates threads within a single process. In a horizontally-scaled deployment, two requests on different pods execute concurrently with no shared lock — only a database-level constraint spans all instances.

assessment.text: What is the correct HTTP status code to return when a replayed idempotency key is detected?
options: A) 409 Conflict — the request conflicts with existing data
B) 201 Created — a new resource was created for the retry
C) 200 OK — return the original response body as if the request just succeeded
D) 422 Unprocessable Entity — the payload is semantically invalid
assessment.explanation: RFC semantics for idempotency require that replayed requests receive the same response as the original successful request. Returning 200 with the original body lets clients safely retry without special-casing duplicate detection logic.

assessment.text: Which of the following correctly describes why a UNIQUE constraint fixes the race where existsByKey() does not?
options: A) The UNIQUE constraint adds a SELECT FOR UPDATE before every INSERT automatically
B) The UNIQUE constraint makes the INSERT itself the atomic gate — the database rejects concurrent duplicate inserts regardless of what the application checked earlier
C) UNIQUE constraints prevent two transactions from opening simultaneously on the same table
D) The constraint forces the application to retry until a slot is available
assessment.explanation: A UNIQUE constraint is enforced atomically by the storage engine at INSERT time. Even if two transactions both pass an earlier application-level check, the database guarantees that only one INSERT with that key value will succeed — there is no race window inside a single atomic statement.

experiments.title: Optimistic Lock Version Conflict
experiments.subtitle: Silent Refund Drop on Stale @Version
experiments.scenario: Two concurrent refund requests load the same account entity at version 5. The first request commits its credit and bumps the version to 6. The second request throws ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException — but without retry logic the exception is logged and swallowed, silently dropping the second refund.
experiments.impact: A customer's refund is confirmed at the API layer (HTTP 200) but never applied to their balance. The customer is effectively denied money they are owed, triggering chargebacks, regulatory complaints, and manual remediation effort.
incorrectCode: // UNSAFE: no retry — stale version silently drops the refund
public void processRefund(Long accountId, BigDecimal refundAmount) {
// If another transaction committed between findById and save,
// Without @Retryable the exception propagates — refund is lost.

incorrectAnnotations.note: UNSAFE: findById() loads the entity at the current version (e.g., version=5). If another transaction commits before save(), this version becomes stale.
UNSAFE: save() will throw ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException if the version in the database no longer matches the loaded entity — and without @Retryable the refund is silently lost.

experiments.failureExplanation: Optimistic locking works by attaching a version number to each entity row. When the application calls save(), the generated UPDATE includes a WHERE version = ? clause; if another transaction has already incremented the version, the UPDATE affects zero rows and Spring Data throws ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException. Without a retry mechanism that re-reads the entity at the new version, the exception terminates the transaction and the refund credit is never persisted — even though the caller may have already received a success response.

// Re-read inside retry so each attempt starts with fresh version
experiments.correctExplanation: @Retryable intercepts ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException and re-enters the method, which begins a new transaction and re-reads the entity at the latest committed version — ensuring the refund is applied on top of whatever state the account is in after the competing transaction.

Under high concurrency on the same account, the retry storm (exponential backoff helps but does not eliminate it) can degrade throughput. Consider falling back to pessimistic locking (SELECT FOR UPDATE) for accounts that frequently receive concurrent updates.

tests.limitations: Thread scheduling may rarely serialise both transactions, making the test pass even without retry. Use a larger pool or a barrier to increase collision probability; also assert that WARN-level retry logs appeared.

assessment.text: What SQL clause does Spring Data JPA add to the UPDATE statement when @Version is used, and what happens if it matches zero rows?
options: A) WHERE id = ? — if no rows match, the update is silently ignored
B) WHERE id = ? AND version = ? — if zero rows are updated, Spring Data throws ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException
C) FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED — if the row is locked, the update skips it
D) ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING — duplicates are silently discarded
assessment.explanation: Spring Data JPA generates UPDATE … SET … WHERE id = ? AND version = ?. If another transaction has already incremented the version, the WHERE clause matches zero rows; the JPA provider detects the zero-row update and throws ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException to signal the stale state.

assessment.text: Why must the entity be re-read inside the @Retryable method body rather than passed in as a parameter?
options: A) Spring @Retryable requires all parameters to be serializable and entities are not
B) If the entity object is reused across retry attempts it still holds the stale version number, so the second attempt will also fail
C) @Transactional clears the entity cache between retries automatically only if re-read is used
D) The @Version field is reset to 0 on retry if passed as a parameter
assessment.explanation: The in-memory entity carries the version number from when it was first loaded. Reusing the same object across retries means the UPDATE again uses the stale version and fails again indefinitely. Re-reading inside the method ensures each attempt starts with the latest committed version from the database.

assessment.text: In what scenario should you switch from @Version optimistic locking to SELECT FOR UPDATE pessimistic locking?
options: A) When the entity has more than five fields
B) When concurrent conflicts are frequent (high contention) and retry storms are degrading throughput
C) When the Spring version is below 5.3
D) When the database is running in READ UNCOMMITTED isolation
assessment.explanation: Optimistic locking performs best when conflicts are rare — retries are cheap because they seldom happen. Under sustained high contention (many writers on the same row), retries amplify database load and latency. Pessimistic locking (SELECT FOR UPDATE) queues writers at the row level, eliminating retries at the cost of reduced parallelism.

experiments.title: JDBC Connection Pool Deadlock
experiments.subtitle: HikariCP Starvation via @Async Inside @Transactional
experiments.scenario: A payment processing service holds a HikariCP connection inside a @Transactional method and calls an @Async audit service that also needs a connection from the same pool. When all pool connections are held by outer transactions waiting for the async calls to complete, no connection is available for the audit tasks — the entire system deadlocks.
experiments.impact: All in-flight payment transactions hang until the connection timeout fires, causing a cascade of 500 errors, missed SLA windows, and potential duplicate payment retries from upstream clients — all without any application exception until the HikariCP timeout threshold is reached.
incorrectCode: // UNSAFE: holds a DB connection AND spawns @Async task needing a connection
// This @Async call submits a task to a thread pool.
// That task will try to acquire its own HikariCP connection.
// If the pool is exhausted (held by outer @Transactional callers),
// the async task blocks → outer transaction never releases → DEADLOCK.
// Needs its own DB connection from the same HikariCP pool

incorrectAnnotations.note: UNSAFE: auditService.recordAuditEvent() is annotated @Async — it submits work to a thread pool, but the outer @Transactional method is still holding a HikariCP connection while waiting for the async method to be accepted.

UNSAFE: AuditService.recordAuditEvent() opens its own @Transactional, requiring another HikariCP connection. If maxPoolSize equals the number of concurrent outer transactions, every audit task blocks waiting for a connection that will never be released.

experiments.failureExplanation: HikariCP maintains a fixed-size connection pool. Each @Transactional payment method acquires one connection and holds it for the transaction's duration. When it calls @Async auditService.recordAuditEvent(), the async task is submitted to a thread pool and immediately tries to acquire its own HikariCP connection. If all pool connections are held by payment transactions waiting for their async tasks (which are queued waiting for connections), neither side can proceed — a circular wait satisfying all four Coffman deadlock conditions. The system hangs until HikariCP's connectionTimeout elapses, then throws SQLTimeoutException.

assessment.text: What are the four Coffman conditions that must all be true for a deadlock, and how does @Async inside @Transactional satisfy them in this scenario?
options: A) Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait — satisfied when T1 holds C1 and waits for C2 while T2 holds C2 and waits for C1

B) Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait — satisfied when payment threads hold connections while async audit threads wait for connections, and audit threads cannot proceed until payment threads release, which won't happen until audit threads complete
C) Starvation, priority inversion, livelock, deadlock — satisfied when low-priority audit threads starve high-priority payment threads
D) Race condition, lost update, dirty read, phantom read — satisfied when MVCC allows concurrent snapshot reads
assessment.explanation: Coffman conditions: (1) Mutual exclusion — connections are exclusive; (2) Hold-and-wait — payment threads hold connections while waiting for async slots; (3) No preemption — connections cannot be forcibly taken; (4) Circular wait — payment threads wait for audit tasks that wait for connections held by payment threads. All four are satisfied, confirming a true deadlock.

assessment.text: Why does @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT) break the deadlock?
options: A) It executes the audit handler before the payment transaction acquires a connection
B) It defers the audit handler until after the payment transaction commits and releases its connection, so the handler never competes with the payment transaction for pool slots
C) It runs the audit handler in the same thread and transaction as the payment, sharing the same connection
D) It disables the connection pool for the audit service entirely
assessment.explanation: AFTER_COMMIT phase means the event handler is invoked only after the publishing transaction has successfully committed — which also means the connection has been returned to the pool. The audit handler then acquires a fresh connection from the now-available pool without any circular dependency.

assessment.text: What is the safest HikariCP configuration to detect connection leaks caused by connections held inside long-running transactions?
options: A) Set maximumPoolSize=1 to force serialisation and surface contention
B) Set leakDetectionThreshold to a value slightly above the expected maximum transaction duration, which logs a warning with the stack trace of any connection held longer
C) Set connectionTimeout=0 to disable timeouts and prevent false alarms
D) Disable HikariCP and use a single shared connection instance
assessment.explanation: leakDetectionThreshold causes HikariCP to log a warning (with the borrowing thread's stack trace) for any connection held longer than the threshold. This surfaces connections leaked inside long transactions without breaking the application, enabling targeted investigation.

experiments.title: Saga Compensation Running Twice
experiments.subtitle: Non-Idempotent Compensation in Distributed Transactions
experiments.scenario: A three-step payment saga (Debit → Reserve → Charge) fails at the Charge step and triggers a compensating un-debit event. Due to at-least-once delivery semantics, the compensation event is delivered a second time by the message broker. The non-idempotent handler credits the account twice, returning more money than was originally debited.
experiments.impact: The customer's account is credited twice for a single failed payment: a direct financial loss to the institution, an audit discrepancy, and a potential regulatory violation if the double-credit is not detected before settlement.

experiments.failureExplanation: Kafka's at-least-once delivery guarantee means consumers can receive the same message more than once, particularly after a rebalance, pod restart, or producer retry. The compensation handler has no memory of previously processed saga IDs, so it treats each delivery as a fresh instruction. When the same UnDebitEvent arrives twice, the account balance is credited twice — once for each delivery — resulting in a double-reversal. Without idempotency guards at the handler level, the saga's compensation step is fundamentally unsafe under the network conditions of a real production system.

assessment.text: Why does Kafka's at-least-once delivery guarantee make compensation handlers non-idempotent by default?
options: A) Kafka encrypts messages differently on each delivery, causing handlers to compute different results

B) At-least-once delivery means the same message can be delivered more than once (after rebalance, restart, or timeout), so a handler that mutates state unconditionally will apply the mutation multiple times
C) Kafka partitions guarantee ordering but not exactly-once semantics only for producers, not consumers
D) Compensation handlers are always called twice by the saga orchestrator as a redundancy mechanism
assessment.explanation: At-least-once delivery is a Kafka consumer contract: messages are guaranteed to be delivered at least once but may be delivered more times due to consumer rebalances, offset commit failures, or producer retries. A handler that applies a balance credit unconditionally will credit the account once per delivery — making idempotency a mandatory design requirement for any state-mutating handler.

assessment.text: Why must the saga_compensations record be inserted in the same transaction as the balance update rather than in a separate transaction after?
options: A) Separate transactions would cause a foreign key violation on the accounts table
B) If the application crashes between the balance update commit and the compensation record insert, the guard will never be written, allowing a future redelivery to apply a second credit
C) Separate transactions are not supported when using @KafkaListener
D) The saga_compensations insert would deadlock with the accounts update if run sequentially
assessment.explanation: Atomicity is essential: if the balance UPDATE commits but the compensation INSERT does not (due to a crash, network partition, or rollback), a subsequent redelivery finds no guard record and applies a duplicate credit. Writing both changes in a single transaction guarantees that either both succeed or both fail, preserving the idempotency invariant.

assessment.text: What additional database constraint provides a last-resort safety net for the saga_compensations idempotency guard even if two threads race past the exists check simultaneously?
options: A) A CHECK constraint on the balance column preventing negative values
B) A UNIQUE constraint on (saga_id, step) in the saga_compensations table, causing the second concurrent INSERT to fail with a DataIntegrityViolationException
C) A NOT NULL constraint on the saga_id column
D) A FOREIGN KEY constraint linking saga_compensations to the payments table
assessment.explanation: Even with an application-level exists check, two concurrent deliveries can both read false before either insert commits — the same check-then-act race as fin-02. A UNIQUE constraint on (saga_id, step) makes the INSERT atomic, so only one thread can succeed; the second receives a constraint violation and can safely return without applying a second credit.

experiments.title: Kafka + DB Dual Write Failure
experiments.subtitle: Transactional Outbox Pattern with Debezium CDC
experiments.scenario: A payment service writes to PostgreSQL and then publishes to Kafka in two separate operations. If the Kafka broker is unavailable after the database commit succeeds, the payment row exists in the database but the downstream settlement and notification services never receive the event — a silent failure with no automatic recovery.
experiments.impact: Payments are processed and funds debited but settlement, fraud detection, and customer notification services never execute — funds are transferred without downstream confirmation, creating reconciliation gaps, missed fraud signals, and customer complaints about missing notifications.

incorrectAnnotations.note: UNSAFE: paymentRepository.save() commits the payment row to the database as part of the @Transactional method. Once committed, there is no way to roll it back if the Kafka send fails.

UNSAFE: kafkaTemplate.send() is a separate network call with no transactional coordination with the database commit on line 21. Any broker exception here leaves the payment in the DB with no corresponding Kafka event.

experiments.failureExplanation: A database transaction and a Kafka produce operation are two independent resources with no shared transaction coordinator (the Kafka transaction protocol is separate from JDBC transactions). When @Transactional commits the database write, the JDBC connection is released — at that point the Kafka send has not yet been issued. If the broker is unavailable, overloaded, or if the application crashes between the two operations, the payment exists in PostgreSQL but no Kafka event is ever produced. There is no built-in retry, no dead-letter queue entry, and no alert — the event is silently lost.

Debezium tails the PostgreSQL WAL, picks up the new outbox row, and publishes to Kafka independently — with its own retry logic — decoupling event publication from the payment transaction lifecycle.

assessment.text: Why does wrapping both paymentRepository.save() and kafkaTemplate.send() in a single @Transactional method NOT guarantee atomicity between the database and Kafka?
options: A) @Transactional only works with JDBC operations and is silently ignored for Kafka calls

B) The database transaction and the Kafka produce operation are separate resources with no shared transaction coordinator; a @Transactional Spring context only manages JDBC transactions by default, leaving Kafka outside its scope
C) KafkaTemplate.send() is always asynchronous and cannot participate in any transaction
D) @Transactional rolls back both resources automatically if kafkaTemplate.send() throws, so there is no data inconsistency
assessment.explanation: Spring's @Transactional manages JDBC resources through a DataSourceTransactionManager. Kafka has its own transaction protocol (KafkaTransactionManager). Without XA (two-phase commit) or a pattern like the Transactional Outbox, these two resources are completely independent — a commit of one does not guarantee a commit of the other.

assessment.text: What is the core guarantee that the Transactional Outbox pattern provides, and how does it achieve it?
options: A) Exactly-once Kafka delivery — by using Kafka's idempotent producer under the hood
B) Atomic write of the domain record and the event record in a single ACID database transaction, ensuring the event is never lost even if Kafka is unavailable at write time
C) Synchronous Kafka delivery within the same HTTP request lifecycle as the database write
D) Automatic rollback of the database transaction if the Kafka broker rejects the event
assessment.explanation: The outbox pattern leverages the database's own ACID guarantees: writing both the payment and the outbox_event in a single transaction means either both are committed or neither is. The event cannot be lost because it is durably stored in the database; the CDC relay (Debezium) publishes it to Kafka independently with its own retry logic.

assessment.text: How does Debezium read the outbox table without additional polling queries, and what database feature does it rely on?
options: A) Debezium issues a SELECT * FROM outbox_events WHERE processed = false every second using a scheduled job
B) Debezium uses PostgreSQL logical replication (the Write-Ahead Log) to stream row changes in real time, with no polling queries and sub-second latency
C) Debezium registers a PostgreSQL trigger on outbox_events that calls a Kafka producer stored procedure
D) Debezium subscribes to Spring application events published by the outbox repository
assessment.explanation: Debezium acts as a PostgreSQL logical replication consumer, reading the Write-Ahead Log (WAL) stream. Every committed INSERT to outbox_events appears in the WAL and is relayed to Kafka by Debezium — with no polling latency, no additional database load from SELECT queries, and built-in backpressure and retry.
